cases.name: no heap base falls back to the fixed control base
a heap base BELOW the fallback still wins
cases.why: 2 MiB is page 32, so channel 33 and control_end 35. This is the case the two hosts disagreed about: crates/host-native ignored __heap_base and answered 256/257/259 here.

cases.name: a heap base ABOVE the fallback keeps control memory off the program's data
cases.why: 32 MiB is page 512. The old native-host rule placed control memory at page 256 — INSIDE this program's own static data — which is the defect this corpus pins.

cases.name: an unaligned heap base rounds UP to a page
cases.why: 2097153 is one byte into page 32, so control memory starts at page 33.

cases.name: a heap base below the default initial pages is raised to that floor
cases.why: 65536 is page 1, below DEFAULT_INITIAL_PAGES (17 pages = 1114112 bytes), so the floor supplies first_free_byte: control_base_page 17, channel 18, control_end 20. No other case in this file sits below the floor, so this is the only case that distinguishes the rule from one that ignores DEFAULT_INITIAL_PAGES entirely.

cases.name: an imported memory minimum above the fallback raises the floor
cases.why: 600 pages is 39321600 bytes, past the 16 MiB fallback, so the floor comes from the import. Marked programBytesOnly: an imported memory's minimum is a fact only a program's bytes carry, so the TypeScript half would have to synthesise a binary to present it. Every other case names its facts directly and both hosts check it.

cases.name: a caller's own minimum raises the floor too
cases.why: 1000 pages is 65536000 bytes; control memory follows at pages 1001..1002.

cases.name: a smaller ceiling is honoured everywhere it appears
cases.why: maximumPages 512 moves brkLimit and maxAddr, and nothing else.

cases.name: a ceiling that exactly fits control memory is accepted
cases.why: The smallest address space this rule can place: the 17-page floor puts control memory at pages 17..19, so initial_pages is 20 and a ceiling of 20 fits it exactly. The refusal is `initial_pages > maximum_pages`, and no other case has the two equal, so this is the case that keeps it from becoming `>=`. brk_base lands exactly at max_addr here, which is legal: control memory fills the memory and nothing is left to allocate.

refusals.name: a ceiling that cannot hold the syscall channel
refusals.why: A ceiling of 2 pages cannot hold the channel's own 2 pages, let alone the control page under them, so the ceiling is refused before any placement arithmetic runs. The guard is `maximum_pages <= CHANNEL_PAGES`, and this case is what pins the `<=`: were it `<`, a ceiling of 2 would fall through to the later refusal and report "initial pages 259 exceed process maximum 2" instead — a true statement that names the wrong problem.

refusals.name: control memory alone past the ceiling
refusals.why: The fallback base needs 259 pages and the ceiling is 100.

refusals.name: control memory past a ceiling near the top of the page space saturates its report
refusals.why: heapBase is exactly maxAddr, so the ceiling check admits it and control memory's last page lands above u32::MAX. A truncated report would say 'initial pages 2', which reads as a request far smaller than the one being refused.

refusals.name: a heap base past the ceiling is refused before the page arithmetic
refusals.why: A program may export any __heap_base at all; 2^63 must refuse, not overflow.

refusals.name: one page short of fitting control memory is refused
refusals.why: The same request with a ceiling of 19. Paired with the accepting case above, it fixes the boundary at exactly 20 rather than near it.
